title: Pie Chart Interpretation
tagline: Year 2 — Sectors, percentages, angles and comparing two pie charts

introduction.overview: A pie chart shows how a total is divided into parts. Each sector's angle at the centre (out of 360°) corresponds to its share of the total. In Year 2 you meet two pie charts side by side, for two years, with different totals. A common trap is comparing percentages across the two charts without taking the totals into account: a smaller percentage of a larger total can be a larger amount.
introduction.placementRelevance: Pie chart sets are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, often with two pies and a request to compare amounts across them.
introduction.realWorldContext: Budget breakdowns, market shares and expense reports are shown as pie charts.

learningObjectives: Convert percentages to angles (× 3.6) and back (÷ 3.6)
Find amounts from share and total
Compare amounts across two pie charts with different totals
Compute percentage change in amounts, not in shares

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Amount = share ÷ 100 × total. Angle = share × 3.6°. Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.

coreDefinitions: Sector: one slice of the pie, representing one category.
Central angle: the angle at the centre; 360° is the whole.
Share: the sector as a percentage of the total.
Percentage points: the difference between two shares (28% to 30% is 2 points).
Absolute amount: share × total; it can rise even when the share falls.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: The pie tells you shares, not amounts. To compare years you must convert each share to an amount using its own total. A share that falls from 30% to 28% can still mean more money if the total has grown.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Make a table of amounts for each year: share × total. Then every comparison is between two cells of this table.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Percentage points
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Not the same as percentage change.

mainNarrative: Start with the shares and the total. In 2022 the total expenditure is ₹5,00,000 and salary is 30%, so the salary amount is ₹1,50,000 and its sector angle is 30 × 3.6 = 108°.
To compare years, build a table of amounts. In 2023 (total ₹6,00,000), salary is 28%, which is ₹1,68,000. So salary rose in amount even though its share fell from 30% to 28%.

Percentage change is computed on amounts. Marketing was 18% of ₹5,00,000 = ₹90,000 and 20% of ₹6,00,000 = ₹1,20,000. The increase is 30,000 ÷ 90,000 = 33.3%, which is larger than that of any other item.
For rent, the shares are 12% and 10%. The amounts are ₹60,000 in both years, so the rent did not change in rupees although its share fell.
For ratios of amounts across the two pies, use the amounts: Salary in 2022 to salary in 2023 is 1,50,000 : 1,68,000 = 25 : 28.

deepDiveAspects.title: Share falls, amount rises
deepDiveAspects.content: If the total grows faster than the share falls, the amount rises. Always compute the amounts before commenting on growth.

deepDiveAspects.title: Angles across pies
deepDiveAspects.content: Angles depend on shares only. The same angle in two pies with different totals stands for different amounts.

solvedExamples.title: Angle and amount
solvedExamples.question: In 2022, salary was 30% of the total expenditure of ₹5,00,000. Find the central angle and the amount.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Angle uses the share; amount uses the total.

solvedExamples.title: Compare amounts across years
solvedExamples.question: By what percentage did the expenditure on marketing increase from 2022 to 2023 (to one decimal place)?

solvedExamples.title: Share falls, amount same
solvedExamples.question: The share of rent fell from 12% to 10%. What happened to the amount spent on rent?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The total grew in the same proportion as the share fell.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Convert each share to an amount using its own total, then compare, take ratios and compute percentage changes on the amounts.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing percentage points and percentage change

commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Use the year of the pie.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: If the totals differ, reject options that compare shares as if they were amounts.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Two-pie sets are mostly about not mixing shares and amounts.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I find an angle from a share?
Can I compare amounts across pies?
Can I compute a percentage change in an amount?
